_meta.title: MeteGPT Evidence Log
_meta.purpose: Every claim about a named competitor tool or AI detector published on metegpt.com links to a dated primary source recorded here; article citations like (EV-winston-ai-detector-01) resolve to the matching id below.
_meta.screening_note: Only sources screened INCLUDED under the protocol appear here. Excluded categories -- off-topic, affiliate roundups with no disclosed methodology, sources unverifiable on the collection run, duplicates, and vendor-seeded 'astroturf' review content -- are withheld by design; the protocol never cites them. Each page's collection_sweep publishes the exclusion COUNTS (including how many sources were screened out as astroturf) so the screening is auditable without republishing any withheld source or naming any third party.
_meta.field_note: Internal working fields (coder identities, curator annotations, flow IDs) are omitted. The citable record for each item is its claim, verbatim quote, source URL and source date.
_meta.cross_listed_note: A source that supports claims on more than one page appears under each; unique_sources counts distinct ids, page_appearances counts listings.

entries.claim: Turnitin itself suppresses AI scores below 20%: since July 8, 2024 no numeric score or highlights are shown for detections above 0% and below 20% — the report shows an asterisk (*%) instead, and Turnitin states the reason is 'to avoid potential incidence of false positives' (vendor's own acknowledgment that low-range scores are too noisy to state precisely)
entries.quote: To avoid potential incidence of false positives, no score or highlights are attributed for AI detection scores above 0% and below the 20% threshold in the report. When this occurs, it is now indicated with an asterisk (*%)
entries.source_date: 2024-07-08 (policy effective date, stated on page; page maintained current as of capture)
entries.platform: turnitin guides (vendor primary source)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN via r.jina.ai reader proxy of helpcenter.turnitin.com/hc/en-us/articles/46245332050317 (direct fetch 403, the documented Turnitin-domain block). Quote 'To avoid potential incidences of false positives, Turnitin does not display specific numerical scores or source highlights for AI detection levels within the 1% to 19% range... An asterisk symbol (*%) is displayed' re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score as the page's ONLY Turnitin band: the under-20% bound, presented as Turnitin's own reporting mechanism (no numeric score attributed below 20%), never a precise figure, always paired with 'the institution sets the threshold, there is no universal safe number.'

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed Stanford study found commercial GPT detectors misclassify non-native-English (TOEFL) essays as AI-written at a much higher rate than native-English essays, supporting the ESL false-positive risk warning.
entries.quote: they incorrectly labeled more than half of the TOEFL essays as 'AI-generated' (average false-positive rate: 61.3%)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (Patterns, Cell Press; Liang et al., DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10382961/, HTTP 200). The 61.3% average TOEFL false-positive quote and DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779 re-read verbatim; the paper's anonymization of its seven tested detectors re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score strictly as the ESL/non-native-English false-positive science that routes reader (a) OUT (a score is a probability, not proof) -- never presented as a single-named-detector result. Written independently of the humanizemy sibling (inter-site dedup).

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) found that no AI-text detection tool it tested reached 80% accuracy, only five of the fourteen surpassed 70%, and the tools showed a systematic bias toward classifying output as human-written rather than AI-generated.
entries.quote: the available detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable... a main bias towards classifying the output as human-written rather than detecting AI-generated text
entries.source_date: 2023-07-10 (v2; journal publication International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26, 2023)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; also on arXiv, Weber-Wulff et al., 8 authors including Debora Weber-Wulff, HTW Berlin)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666). Abstract quote 'the available detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable... a main bias towards classifying the output as human-written rather than detecting AI-generated text' re-confirmed verbatim; Weber-Wulff et al., Int. J. for Educational Integrity Vol 19 Art 26 (2023) confirmed. NOTE: the body figures ('no tool reached 80% accuracy, only five of fourteen surpassed 70%') live in the paper body, not the abstract, and were NOT re-read this run (last body-verified 2026-07-07, unchanged since); flagged. Extended to /good-ai-score for the 'detectors disagree, so no single number is universal' point.

entries.claim: The same peer-reviewed 14-tool study found that content-obfuscation techniques (paraphrasing/editing AI text) significantly worsen detector performance across the tools tested — direct academic support for the 'paraphrased/humanized text lowers reliability' disclosure this page must make about detectors generally, including pattern-based ones.
entries.quote: Content obfuscation techniques significantly worsen the performance of tools
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; Weber-Wulff et al. 2023)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666). Quote 'content obfuscation techniques significantly worsen the performance of tools' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /ai-detector-accuracy as academic support for the 'accuracy is conditional (paraphrased/edited text lowers reliability)' section.

entries.claim: A 2025 NBER/Becker Friedman Institute working paper (Jabarian & Imas) comparing four AI-text detectors on 1,992 human and 1,992 AI-generated passages across six genres found the three commercial tools (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) held false-positive rates under 1% on medium/long text, but the open-source RoBERTa baseline misclassified human text at a 30-78% false-positive rate depending on scenario — concrete cross-detector evidence that detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, not just marketing claims.
entries.quote: false positive rates of approximately 30-78% across scenarios [for RoBERTa]... All three commercial tools maintained false positive rates below 1 percent [on medium/long passages]
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; underlying NBER Working Paper No. 34223, authors Brian Jabarian and Alex Imas)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/, page still dated 2025-10-06). RoBERTa 'false positive rates of approximately 30-78%' and the three commercial tools' 'essentially zero false positive rates... on medium-length to long passages' both re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score: detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, so a 'good score' on one tool is not the same on another.

entries.claim: The same NBER/BFI study found accuracy for all three commercial detectors (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) degrades on short passages, with texts under roughly 50 words the hardest case for every tool tested — direct academic corroboration of the 'short text is a structurally noisy signal for any detector' disclosure this page must make.
entries.quote: Accuracy varied significantly by text length, with short passages (under 50 words) proving most challenging
entries.platform: university business-school research review (Chicago Booth Review, summarizing Jabarian & Imas / NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (chicagobooth.edu/review/do-ai-detectors-work-well-enough-trust, still dated 2025-12-02). Short-passage-difficulty finding re-confirmed; live wording 'Because shorter passages give the detectors less to analyze, they tend to be more challenging to correctly identify' remains a paraphrase-equivalent of the registered quote (standing 2026-07-07 flag). 'All three commercial tools kept false positive rates below 1 percent, with Pangram's the lowest' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score as the academic basis for the honest short-text caveat (the free-tier 125-word-per-run reality: a short passage is a structurally noisier signal for any detector).

entries.claim: The same study found GPTZero and Originality.ai occupy a 'secondary tier' relative to Pangram, with a real tradeoff between them: minimizing false positives favors GPTZero, while maximizing detection of AI-written text favors Originality.ai — concrete evidence that different named detectors optimize for different error types, which is the academic basis for recommending a cross-check with a second, differently-tuned detector rather than trusting one tool's verdict.
entries.quote: OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI.
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/). 'OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score: different detectors optimize for different error types, so there is no single cross-detector 'good number.'

entries.claim: Turnitin's own Chief Product Officer publicly acknowledged in June 2023 that real-world detector performance diverged from lab testing, and Turnitin responded by raising its minimum evaluable word count from 150 to 300 words, alongside disclosing a 'higher incidence of false positives' below the 20% AI-writing threshold — an independent journalism account of the same admission EV-turnitin-03 references secondhand.
entries.quote: Chechitelli said Turnitin "discovered real-world use is yielding different results from our lab."
entries.platform: K-12 Dive (education-industry journalism)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (k12dive.com/news/turnitin-false-positives-AI-detector/652221/, dated 2023-06-07). Chechitelli 'discovered real-world use is yielding different results from our lab' re-confirmed verbatim, plus the 150-to-300-word minimum increase and Turnitin's admission of higher false positives below the 20% AI-writing threshold. Extended to /ai-detector-accuracy as evidence that detector performance drifts between lab and real-world conditions (accuracy is not a fixed number).

entries.claim: A university teaching-center resource (University of Kansas Center for Teaching Excellence) documents Turnitin's own March-2023 'AI Writing FAQs' materials disclosing a margin of error of roughly plus-or-minus 15 percentage points on its AI-detection score, plus a Turnitin AI scientist's on-record caution that predictions should be taken 'with a big grain of salt' -- a vendor's own against-interest admission about score imprecision, relayed via a third-party academic source rather than adopted from vendor marketing copy.
entries.quote: Turnitin's tool 'appears to have a margin of error of plus or minus 15 percentage points' ... 'You, the instructor, have to make the final interpretation.'
entries.source_date: 2023-04 (page describes Turnitin's April 2023 AI-detector activation; margin-of-error figure attributed to Turnitin's own 'AI Writing FAQs March 2023' materials)
entries.platform: University of Kansas Center for Teaching Excellence (university teaching-center guidance page, live-verified 2026-07-07)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (cte.ku.edu/careful-use-ai-detectors). Turnitin 'margin of error of plus or minus 15 percentage points' (attributed to Turnitin's AI Writing FAQs, March 2023), 'You, the instructor, have to make the final interpretation,' and David Adamson's (Turnitin AI scientist) 'big grain of salt' caution all re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score as the load-bearing anchor for 'the instructor/institution sets the threshold, and the score itself is noisy (plus-or-minus 15 points), not a universal line.' The plus-or-minus-15pt figure is Turnitin's own self-disclosed material relayed by KU CTE -- cite as such, not as an independent third-party measurement.

entries.quote: Even though Johannes wrote every word himself, ZeroGPT still marked the piece as AI-generated by 66.64%.

entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (academichelp.net/ai-detectors/zerogpt-review.html; published 2023-08-10, updated 2026-03-25). entries.claim: Of 4 answers on a screened Quora thread asking which AI detector is most accurate (fetched 2026-07-22), no two answerers named the same tool: separate answers recommend ZeroGPT, Winston AI, and a bundle of 'Undetectable AI, GPTZero, OpenAI AI Text Classifier and Copyleaks,' while a fourth (a vendor account) redirects to its own product — a documented case of community non-consensus on 'most accurate,' not a ranked verdict.
entries.quote: The best one I've personally used is ZeroGPT. It's easy to use and highlights the parts of the text that look AI-generated. (Clive Herrera, Mar 20) / Winston AI is one of the best AI detectors available... more structured and transparent probability analysis. (Hazel, Mar 25) / Undetectable AI and GPTZero and OpenAI AI Text Classifier and Copyleaks AI Detector stand out as reliable options. (unattributed answer) / Ha ha ha ha no [detectors cannot reliably distinguish AI text]. (Franklin Veaux)
entries.source_date: answers dated 2026-01-12, 2026-03-20, 2026-03-25 and undated (Franklin Veaux, 'updated Sat' relative to 2026-07-22 capture); page live-fetched 2026-07-22
entries.platform: Quora (multiple independent answerers on one question thread)
entries.re_verified_note: RECONFIRMED LIVE THIS RUN via r.jina.ai reader proxy (direct quora.com fetch 403). Core claim -- community non-consensus on the 'most accurate' detector, no two answerers naming the same single tool -- re-confirmed; this run the thread surfaced ZeroGPT (Clive Herrera, 'highlights the parts of the text that look AI-generated, not just a score'), Winston AI (Hazel, 'more structured and transparent probability analysis'), and TraceGPT/PlagiarismCheck.org; 4 answers visible. The thread's answer set is dynamic (documented). Extended to /good-ai-score: if the field cannot agree which detector is 'most accurate,' there is no universal cross-detector 'good score.' Denominator = 4 answers on this thread, never a population percentage.

entries.quote: the same paragraph fed into GPTZero, ZeroGPT, Originality.ai, and Copyleaks routinely produces four different scores. Sometimes by 50 percentage points.
entries.source_date: 2026-05-24 (answer date, per Quora's current-year relative-date display, captured 2026-07-22)
entries.platform: Quora (Lucas Goldfarb, college student)
entries.re_verified_note: RECONFIRMED LIVE THIS RUN via r.jina.ai reader proxy (direct quora.com fetch 403). entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested the same set of human-written, machine-translated, and AI-generated documents across 14 detection tools and found the tools disagree sharply with each other on identical input: the false-positive risk on the same human-written/machine-translated documents ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero), and the false-negative risk on the same AI-generated documents ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale) -- direct, quantified, peer-reviewed evidence of cross-detector inconsistency on the same text.
entries.quote: The probability of false positives ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero). The probability of false negatives ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale).
entries.source_date: 2023-12-04 (journal publication, International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26); arXiv preprint v2 posted 2023-07-10 (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; also on arXiv, Weber-Wulff et al., 8 authors including Debora Weber-Wulff, HTW Berlin) -- same underlying paper as EV-detect-01/EV-detect-02, this entry registers the section-5.1.2/5.2.1 cross-tool-disagreement finding on the SAME 14-tool, same-document-set test, which was not previously captured in the registry
entries.re_verified_note: Attempted live re-fetch this run via the arXiv abstract page (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666): the abstract re-confirms Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck were among the 14 tools tested ('12 publicly available tools and two commercial systems (Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck)') but the section-5 quantified ranges (false positives 0% Turnitin to 50% GPT Zero; false negatives 8% GPT Zero to 100% Content at Scale) live in the paper body, which exceeds the fetch size limit this run (same recurring limitation as the 2026-08-09, 2026-08-13, and 2026-08-15 runs). web.archive.org is fully blocked at the tool level this run (cannot be used as an alternate route). Record rests on its earlier verified capture for the ranges, disclosed. Extended to /turnitin-ai-checker as the strongest peer-reviewed, quantified source naming Turnitin's own measured false-positive rate (0%) alongside its cross-detector context, for the new 'is Turnitin's detector model-specific' section.

entries.claim: A 2025 preprint testing AI detectors on 'AI-polished' writing found that detectors over-flag even minimally edited text as AI-generated and cannot reliably distinguish degrees of AI involvement -- direct evidence that a detector score reflects surface statistical pattern rather than a clean human-versus-AI verdict, and that lightly-edited human writing is a structural false-positive risk.
entries.quote: detectors frequently flag even minimally polished text as AI-generated, struggle to differentiate between degrees of AI involvement
entries.platform: preprint (arXiv 2502.15666; Shoumik Saha and Soheil Feizi, University of Maryland) -- NOT peer-reviewed; must be labeled a preprint wherever cited
entries.re_verified_note: Collected and verified LIVE this run: arxiv.org/abs/2502.15666 fetched HTTP 200; abstract quote read verbatim. Fresh source not used by the humanizemy sibling (not among the six inter-site landmines), so it strengthens the non-dedup position. On-page use: support for 'What Changes an AI Detector's Accuracy?' (conditional accuracy) and the probability-not-verdict / false-positive framing. NOT a bypass claim -- the finding is that detectors OVER-flag lightly-edited text, an honest-limit/false-positive point. Label as a preprint.

entries.claim: Cornell University's Center for Teaching Innovation advises instructors NOT to use current automatic AI-detection tools for academic-integrity decisions, stating the tools are unreliable, cannot provide evidence for their own claims, and show significant margins of error -- an institutional teaching-center source (not a detector vendor) supporting that a single AI-detection score should not be treated as conclusive proof of misconduct.
entries.quote: We currently do not recommend using current automatic detection algorithms for academic integrity violations using generative AI, given their unreliability. ... Detection tools claim to identify work as AI generated, but cannot provide evidence for that claim, and tests have revealed significant margins of error.
entries.platform: university teaching-center guidance (Cornell University Center for Teaching Innovation) -- institutional third party, not a vendor
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (teaching.cornell.edu/generative-artificial-intelligence/ai-academic-integrity). Cornell CTI's recommendation against using current automatic detection algorithms for integrity decisions re-confirmed; live wording 'We currently do not recommend using current automatic detection algorithms for academic integrity violations using generative AI, given their unreliability and current inability to provide definitive evidence of violations' plus 'cannot provide evidence for that claim, and tests have revealed significant margins of error' re-read live. Page carries no explicit date (references 2023 sources) -- cite as 'Cornell CTI guidance, captured 2026-08-15.' Extended to /good-ai-score as an institutional teaching-center source that a single detection score is not conclusive and there is no automatic threshold; written in our own sentence, distinct from the sibling site's institution list (inter-site landmine).

entries.claim: A 2025 peer-reviewed survey of AI-generated-text detection concludes that detectability is CONDITIONAL -- determined by multiple interacting factors and scenarios rather than a single fixed rate -- direct academic support for the thesis that there is no one AI-detector 'accuracy number' and that reliability depends on both the text and the tool.
entries.quote: we aim to provide insight into the salient factors that combine to determine how "detectable" AIGT text is under different scenarios
entries.source_date: 2024-06-21 (revised 2025-04-14; published Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Vol. 82, 2025)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Vol. 82, 2025; also arXiv 2406.15583; Kathleen C. Fraser, Hillary Dawkins, Svetlana Kiritchenko, National Research Council Canada)
entries.re_verified_note: Collected and verified LIVE this run: the exact abstract was read verbatim from arxiv.org/abs/2406.15583v2 (the PDF fetch returned unreadable binary, so the quote was captured from the abstract HTML, HTTP 200). Peer-reviewed status confirmed: published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Vol. 82 (2025). Fresh source not used by the humanizemy sibling. On-page use: 'What Changes an AI Detector's Accuracy?' -- the academic anchor for 'accuracy is conditional, there is no single number'.

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested the same set of human-written, machine-translated, and AI-generated documents across 14 detection tools and found the tools disagree sharply with each other on identical input: the false-positive risk on the same human-written/machine-translated documents ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero), and the false-negative risk on the same AI-generated documents ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale) -- direct, quantified, peer-reviewed evidence of cross-detector inconsistency on the same text.
entries.quote: The probability of false positives ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero). The probability of false negatives ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale).

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested the same set of human-written, machine-translated, and AI-generated documents across 14 detection tools and found the tools disagree sharply with each other on identical input: the false-positive risk on the same human-written/machine-translated documents ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero), and the false-negative risk on the same AI-generated documents ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale) -- direct, quantified, peer-reviewed evidence of cross-detector inconsistency on the same text.
entries.quote: The probability of false positives ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero). The probability of false negatives ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale).
entries.source_date: 2023-12-04 (journal publication, International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26); arXiv preprint v2 posted 2023-07-10 (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; also on arXiv, Weber-Wulff et al., 8 authors including Debora Weber-Wulff, HTW Berlin) -- same underlying paper as EV-detect-01/EV-detect-02, this entry registers the section-5.1.2/5.2.1 cross-tool-disagreement finding on the SAME 14-tool, same-document-set test, which was not previously captured in the registry
entries.re_verified_note: Attempted live re-fetch this run via the arXiv abstract page (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666): the abstract re-confirms Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck were among the 14 tools tested ('12 publicly available tools and two commercial systems (Turnitin and PlagiarismCheck)') but the section-5 quantified ranges (false positives 0% Turnitin to 50% GPT Zero; false negatives 8% GPT Zero to 100% Content at Scale) live in the paper body, which exceeds the fetch size limit this run (same recurring limitation as the 2026-08-09, 2026-08-13, and 2026-08-15 runs). web.archive.org is fully blocked at the tool level this run (cannot be used as an alternate route). Record rests on its earlier verified capture for the ranges, disclosed. Extended to /turnitin-ai-checker as the strongest peer-reviewed, quantified source naming Turnitin's own measured false-positive rate (0%) alongside its cross-detector context, for the new 'is Turnitin's detector model-specific' section.

entries.claim: Turnitin's own primary press release (Aug 27, 2025) announced its AI writing detection expanded to include "AI bypasser detection" capabilities specifically designed to identify text intentionally modified by AI humanizer tools, with Chief Product Officer Annie Chechitelli stating the company updated its software "to detect leading AI bypasser modifications" in response to a new category of "cheating providers" offering humanizers to conceal AI-generated content.
entries.quote: While cheating has always been a concern of educators, with the rise of AI, there has been a new category formed of cheating providers. These companies exist to profit from students' misuse of AI by providing free and easy access to humanizers to conceal AI-generated content. In service of our ongoing commitment to AI writing transparency, we've updated our software to detect leading AI bypasser modifications so educators can uphold academic integrity against this emerging challenge.
entries.platform: Turnitin company press release (primary source; direct automated fetch returns HTTP 403, verified this run via r.jina.ai read-proxy, which returned the full release text)

entries.claim: Purdue University's own announcement of Turnitin's AI writing detection rollout (Mar 2023) states plainly that the AI writing detection indicator and report display only to instructors and are not visible to students -- the structural, still-current reason a student cannot self-check a live Turnitin AI score the way they can with a self-serve detector.
entries.quote: The AI writing detection indicator and report will only display to instructors and is not visible to students.
entries.platform: Purdue University Online (university news page, primary institutional source)

entries.claim: Arcadia University's own IT helpdesk guidance corroborates that Turnitin's AI Writing Report is, by default, visible only to instructors and administrators (not students) so scores can be interpreted with context before any sharing decision -- a second, more recently published institutional source for the same instructor-only visibility rule Purdue states (EV-turnitin-16).
entries.quote: By default, the AI Writing Report is only visible to instructors and administrators to ensure scores are interpreted with context before being shared.
entries.source_date: not disclosed on page (captured 2026-08-05); the article ID (462...) is from a 2026-generation helpdesk platform, indicating the rule is stated as current well after Purdue's 2023 announcement, not a stale repost of it
entries.platform: Arcadia University IT helpdesk (university primary source)

entries.claim: A Temple University Student Success Center / Center for the Advancement of Teaching study (dated 2023-08-14) tested Turnitin's AI writing indicator against a disclosed set of 120 texts across four categories (30 each: fully human, fully AI-generated, 'disguised'/paraphrased AI, and hybrid human+AI) and found accuracy fell from 93% on human-written text to 63% on disguised (paraphrased) AI text and 43% on hybrid text, concluding the tool's flagged sections showed 'no relationship at all' to the text's actual AI-written portions. This predates Turnitin's Aug-2025 AI bypasser retrain (EV-turnitin-15) and must be read as describing the earlier classifier, not current behavior.
entries.quote: the summative scores that Turnitin produced for hybrid texts were markedly inaccurate ... there was no relationship at all between sections flagged as AI generated and parts that actually were AI generated
entries.platform: Temple University Student Success Center and Center for the Advancement of Teaching (disclosed-methodology institutional study, PDF report; authors Lori Salem, Stephanie Fiore, Stephen Kelly, Benjamin Brock)

entries.claim: A Feb-2026 peer-reviewed study (Hadra, Cambridge & Mesbah, published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested Turnitin and Originality against a balanced 192-text set (authentic EFL student writing, professional human writing, AI-generated, and hybrid compositions) and found Turnitin's macro-averaged accuracy was 0.61 (versus Originality's 0.69), concluding neither detector 'achieves the level of reliability required for high-stakes decision-making' and that current tools are 'unsuitable as authoritative arbiters of authorship.'
entries.quote: Originality outperformed Turnitin in overall accuracy (0.69 vs. 0.61). ... Current limitations render them unsuitable as authoritative arbiters of authorship.
entries.source_date: 2026 (published online; International Journal for Educational Integrity, DOI 10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1; underlying testing conducted January-May 2025 per the paper's methodology)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity, Springer)

entries.claim: The University of Texas at Austin Provost's Office states the university does not endorse AI-detection software and, absent a university contract or purchase order, prohibits third-party AI-detection software (which would cover an instructor independently running an AI-detector on student work outside an institutional license) from being used to evaluate student work.

entries.platform: University of Texas at Austin, Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost (university primary source)

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) found that no AI-text detection tool it tested reached 80% accuracy, only five of the fourteen surpassed 70%, and the tools showed a systematic bias toward classifying output as human-written rather than AI-generated.
entries.quote: the available detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable... a main bias towards classifying the output as human-written rather than detecting AI-generated text

entries.claim: A 2025 NBER/Becker Friedman Institute working paper (Jabarian & Imas) comparing four AI-text detectors on 1,992 human and 1,992 AI-generated passages across six genres found the three commercial tools (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) held false-positive rates under 1% on medium/long text, but the open-source RoBERTa baseline misclassified human text at a 30-78% false-positive rate depending on scenario — concrete cross-detector evidence that detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, not just marketing claims.
entries.quote: false positive rates of approximately 30-78% across scenarios [for RoBERTa]... All three commercial tools maintained false positive rates below 1 percent [on medium/long passages]
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; underlying NBER Working Paper No. 34223, authors Brian Jabarian and Alex Imas)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/, page still dated 2025-10-06). RoBERTa 'false positive rates of approximately 30-78%' and the three commercial tools' 'essentially zero false positive rates... on medium-length to long passages' both re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score: detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, so a 'good score' on one tool is not the same on another.

entries.claim: The same NBER/BFI study found accuracy for all three commercial detectors (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) degrades on short passages, with texts under roughly 50 words the hardest case for every tool tested — direct academic corroboration of the 'short text is a structurally noisy signal for any detector' disclosure this page must make.
entries.quote: Accuracy varied significantly by text length, with short passages (under 50 words) proving most challenging
entries.platform: university business-school research review (Chicago Booth Review, summarizing Jabarian & Imas / NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (chicagobooth.edu/review/do-ai-detectors-work-well-enough-trust, still dated 2025-12-02). Short-passage-difficulty finding re-confirmed; live wording 'Because shorter passages give the detectors less to analyze, they tend to be more challenging to correctly identify' remains a paraphrase-equivalent of the registered quote (standing 2026-07-07 flag). 'All three commercial tools kept false positive rates below 1 percent, with Pangram's the lowest' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score as the academic basis for the honest short-text caveat (the free-tier 125-word-per-run reality: a short passage is a structurally noisier signal for any detector).

entries.claim: The same study found GPTZero and Originality.ai occupy a 'secondary tier' relative to Pangram, with a real tradeoff between them: minimizing false positives favors GPTZero, while maximizing detection of AI-written text favors Originality.ai — concrete evidence that different named detectors optimize for different error types, which is the academic basis for recommending a cross-check with a second, differently-tuned detector rather than trusting one tool's verdict.
entries.quote: OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI.
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/). 'OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score: different detectors optimize for different error types, so there is no single cross-detector 'good number.'

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested the same set of human-written, machine-translated, and AI-generated documents across 14 detection tools and found the tools disagree sharply with each other on identical input: the false-positive risk on the same human-written/machine-translated documents ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero), and the false-negative risk on the same AI-generated documents ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale) -- direct, quantified, peer-reviewed evidence of cross-detector inconsistency on the same text.
entries.quote: The probability of false positives ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero). The probability of false negatives ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale).
entries.source_date: 2023-12-04 (journal publication, International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26); arXiv preprint v2 posted 2023-07-10 (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666)

entries.claim: Cornell University's Center for Teaching Innovation advises instructors NOT to use current automatic AI-detection tools for academic-integrity decisions, stating the tools are unreliable, cannot provide evidence for their own claims, and show significant margins of error -- an institutional teaching-center source (not a detector vendor) supporting that a single AI-detection score should not be treated as conclusive proof of misconduct.

entries.claim: A 2025 NBER/Becker Friedman Institute working paper (Jabarian & Imas) comparing four AI-text detectors on 1,992 human and 1,992 AI-generated passages across six genres found the three commercial tools (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) held false-positive rates under 1% on medium/long text, but the open-source RoBERTa baseline misclassified human text at a 30-78% false-positive rate depending on scenario — concrete cross-detector evidence that detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, not just marketing claims.
entries.quote: false positive rates of approximately 30-78% across scenarios [for RoBERTa]... All three commercial tools maintained false positive rates below 1 percent [on medium/long passages]
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; underlying NBER Working Paper No. 34223, authors Brian Jabarian and Alex Imas)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/, page still dated 2025-10-06). RoBERTa 'false positive rates of approximately 30-78%' and the three commercial tools' 'essentially zero false positive rates... on medium-length to long passages' both re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score: detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, so a 'good score' on one tool is not the same on another.

entries.claim: The same NBER/BFI study found accuracy for all three commercial detectors (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) degrades on short passages, with texts under roughly 50 words the hardest case for every tool tested — direct academic corroboration of the 'short text is a structurally noisy signal for any detector' disclosure this page must make.
entries.quote: Accuracy varied significantly by text length, with short passages (under 50 words) proving most challenging
entries.platform: university business-school research review (Chicago Booth Review, summarizing Jabarian & Imas / NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (chicagobooth.edu/review/do-ai-detectors-work-well-enough-trust, still dated 2025-12-02). Short-passage-difficulty finding re-confirmed; live wording 'Because shorter passages give the detectors less to analyze, they tend to be more challenging to correctly identify' remains a paraphrase-equivalent of the registered quote (standing 2026-07-07 flag). 'All three commercial tools kept false positive rates below 1 percent, with Pangram's the lowest' re-confirmed verbatim. Extended to /good-ai-score as the academic basis for the honest short-text caveat (the free-tier 125-word-per-run reality: a short passage is a structurally noisier signal for any detector).

entries.claim: The same study found GPTZero and Originality.ai occupy a 'secondary tier' relative to Pangram, with a real tradeoff between them: minimizing false positives favors GPTZero, while maximizing detection of AI-written text favors Originality.ai — concrete evidence that different named detectors optimize for different error types, which is the academic basis for recommending a cross-check with a second, differently-tuned detector rather than trusting one tool's verdict.
entries.quote: OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI.
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; NBER Working Paper No. 34223)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (bfi.uchicago.edu/insights/artificial-writing-and-automated-detection/). entries.claim: The primary academic source behind the widely-cited 'near-zero Pangram false positives' claim (Jabarian & Imas, published directly at chicagobooth.edu) tested roughly 2,000 human-written passages across four length bands (very short under 50 words, short 80-130, medium 200-500, long about 1,000 words) and found Pangram's accuracy never dropped below 99.8%, with false positives 'essentially 0 across most decision thresholds' -- a materially different sample description than The Atlantic's own paraphrase of the same study ('some 3,000 sample texts of roughly 500 to 1,000 words'). This page verified the primary source directly rather than repeating the secondary paraphrase.
entries.quote: Pangram's accuracy was 100 percent for most models and types of writing, and never lower than 99.8 percent... Pangram did best, making almost no mistakes [on false positives]... essentially 0 across most decision thresholds.

entries.claim: RAID (Robust AI Detection), the benchmark QuillBot cites as its accuracy source, is a peer-reviewed academic paper (ACL 2024) covering 11 generative models, 8 content domains, 11 adversarial attacks and 4 decoding strategies, with a public leaderboard that is explicitly split into two sections -- detectors that self-report training on the RAID dataset, and detectors that do not -- specifically to separate in-domain from out-of-domain performance.
entries.quote: The leaderboard is split up into two sections—one for those who self-report having trained on the RAID dataset and one for those who do not. This is important to ensure that a clear distinction is made between detectors that are generalizing to out-of-domain data and those that are not.
entries.platform: peer-reviewed academic paper (ACL 2024; authors Dugan, Hwang, Trhlik, Ludan, Zhu, Xu, Ippolito, Callison-Burch)

entries.claim: QuillBot's own submission to the RAID leaderboard (dated 2025-01-30) reports an aggregate true-positive rate of 99.62% at a fixed 5% false-positive operating point and 98.10% at a fixed 1% false-positive operating point -- these, not a single unconditional 99% figure, are the actual figures behind QuillBot's marketed '99% detection rate.'
entries.platform: primary-source benchmark submission data (github.com/liamdugan/raid, the official RAID repository underlying raid-bench.xyz; QuillBot's own self-submitted results file)

entries.claim: QuillBot's RAID submission calibrates a separate detection threshold for each of RAID's 8 content domains to hit the same fixed false-positive rate, and those thresholds span roughly four orders of magnitude -- from 0.000126 for academic abstracts to 0.936 for product/service reviews at the 5%-false-positive setting -- meaning QuillBot's detector requires a far stronger raw AI-signal in review-style text than in abstract-style text before it will flag either as AI-generated.
entries.platform: primary-source benchmark submission data (github.com/liamdugan/raid; QuillBot's own self-submitted results file)

entries.claim: Within QuillBot's own RAID submission, performance is not uniform across attack types: at the stricter 1%-false-positive operating point, the aggregated true-positive rate for AI text rewritten by RAID's 'paraphrase' adversarial attack is 94.07%, and for text modified with 'zero_width_space' insertions is 91.39% -- both below the submission's own 98.10% aggregate figure at that same threshold.
entries.quote: attack: paraphrase, domain: all, model: all, FPR 0.01 aggregate: tp 204704 / fn 12896 / total 217600 = 94.07%; attack: zero_width_space, FPR 0.01 aggregate: tp 198884 / fn 18716 / total 217600 = 91.39%
entries.platform: primary-source benchmark submission data (github.com/liamdugan/raid; QuillBot's own self-submitted results file)

entries.claim: GPTZero -- a competing AI-detector vendor -- publishes its own dated review of QuillBot's detector citing 'Independent tests done by journalists put QuillBot at around 80% accuracy,' hyperlinked directly to the same ZDNet article that, when re-fetched live at that exact URL, currently shows QuillBot scoring 100%, not 80% -- illustrating that a single detector-accuracy figure sourced from an ongoing test can go stale relative to its own cited source well before a citing page itself is updated.
entries.quote: Independent tests done by journalists put QuillBot at around 80% accuracy, although as with all AI detection tools, results depend on the type of text
entries.platform: competing detector vendor review (gptzero.me; a rival AI detector publishing a review of QuillBot; byline 'GPTZero Team', no individual named)

entries.claim: A competing writing-extension vendor's disclosed 50-text comparison test scored QuillBot's detector at approximately 80% accuracy, behind GPTZero (99.5%) and Scribbr (84%) in the same comparison, and separately notes QuillBot's detector struggles with paraphrased AI content and inputs under 80 words.

It works best on longer texts but struggles with paraphrased AI content and short inputs under 80 words.

entries.quote: QuillBot flagged a 300-word blog introduction as mostly AI-written [raw ChatGPT]; a genuinely human-authored piece was flagged as partially AI-generated; material with approximately 40% manual rewrites was classified as looks human
entries.platform: independent tech writer (Medium; author Himanshu Kumar, bylined; not a competing detector or humanizer vendor)

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed Stanford study found commercial GPT detectors misclassify non-native-English (TOEFL) essays as AI-written at a much higher rate than native-English essays, supporting the ESL false-positive risk warning.
entries.quote: they incorrectly labeled more than half of the TOEFL essays as 'AI-generated' (average false-positive rate: 61.3%)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (Patterns, Cell Press; Liang et al., DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779)
entries.re_verified_note: RE-VERIFIED LIVE THIS RUN (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10382961/, HTTP 200). The 61.3% average TOEFL false-positive quote and DOI 10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779 re-read verbatim; the paper's anonymization of its seven tested detectors re-confirmed. Extended to /good-ai-score strictly as the ESL/non-native-English false-positive science that routes reader (a) OUT (a score is a probability, not proof) -- never presented as a single-named-detector result. Written independently of the humanizemy sibling (inter-site dedup).

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed study from Texas A&M University's Department of Entomology (published in Instars: A Journal of Student Research, an undergraduate-emphasis peer-reviewed venue) tested Sapling's AI detector on 20 human-written, 20 ChatGPT-generated, and 20 hybrid writing samples (10 repeated trials each). Sapling identified 100% of the AI-generated samples (zero variance across all 20 samples, all 10 trials). On the human-written samples, 18 of 20 (90%) received a nonzero AI-detection score -- the figure the paper's own abstract reports as its false-positive rate -- while the mean AI-detection score across all 20 human samples was 25.8% (SD 33.03%), and only 2 of 20 samples scored a literal 0%.
entries.quote: It was determined that, while Sapling could identify AI-generated samples with 100% accuracy, it struggled to accurately identify human-written text, with 90% resulting in a false positive.
entries.platform: peer-reviewed student-research journal (Instars: A Journal of Student Research, Vol. 9 No. 1, Texas A&M University Dept. of Entomology; journal policy requires 2 subject-matter reviewers + 2 writing-craft reviewers per submission)

entries.claim: Sapling's own AI-detector product page states, in its own words, that no AI content detector -- including its own -- should be treated as a standalone determination of AI authorship, and that false positives and false negatives will occur.
entries.quote: No current AI content detector (including Sapling's) should be used as a standalone check to determine whether text is AI-generated or written by a human. False positives and false negatives will occur.
entries.platform: vendor primary source (sapling.ai) -- self-interested, but a credit-due admission against its own product's reliability

entries.claim: Sapling's own FAQ warns its users against AI-humanizer / bypass tools that claim to defeat its detector, stating it has seen such tools falsely claim a 'passed' result even when no check was performed by Sapling.ai.
entries.quote: We've seen such tools make false claims such as that a text "passed" Sapling.ai's detector even though no check was performed by Sapling.ai. Please be careful when using such tools.
entries.platform: vendor primary source (sapling.ai)

entries.claim: VENDOR CLAIM: Sapling's own AI-detector page states 97%+ detection on AI-generated content and under 3% false positives on human-written content, based on 'our benchmarks using longer texts' -- no sample size, dataset composition, or test date is published alongside the claim.
entries.quote: On our benchmarks using longer texts: 97%+ detection rate for AI-generated content. Less than 3% false positive rate for human-written content.

entries.claim: aidetector.ac's benchmark (dated March 2026; 2,400 samples: 1,200 human-written across 5 content categories + 1,200 AI-generated from Claude 3.5/GPT-4o/Gemini 1.5 Pro/Llama 3.1) reports Sapling AI at 76% overall accuracy, 17% false-positive rate, and 24% false-negative rate -- the lowest overall accuracy and highest false-positive rate of the 6 detectors it tested (vs. 91%/7% for its top-ranked tool, Originality.ai). The same benchmark's category breakdown separately states Sapling flagged 31% of human-written technical documentation as AI, its highest false-positive category.
entries.quote: Accuracy from testing on 2,400 samples: 1,200 human-written and 1,200 AI-generated from Claude 3.5, GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Llama 3.1.

entries.claim: DecEptioner's own blog (a company selling an AI-bypass/humanizer tool) tested Sapling against a 160-sample CSV (78 human-written, 82 AI-generated) and reports 63.1% overall accuracy, a 66.7% false-positive rate on the human-written samples (52 of 78 misclassified as AI), 62.4% balanced accuracy, and a 0.716 ROC AUC -- authored and published by Shadab Sayeed, who identifies himself in the same post as CEO & Founder of DecEptioner.

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested the same set of human-written, machine-translated, and AI-generated documents across 14 detection tools and found the tools disagree sharply with each other on identical input: the false-positive risk on the same human-written/machine-translated documents ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero), and the false-negative risk on the same AI-generated documents ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale) -- direct, quantified, peer-reviewed evidence of cross-detector inconsistency on the same text.
entries.quote: The probability of false positives ranged from 0% (Turnitin) to 50% (GPT Zero). The probability of false negatives ranged from 8% (GPT Zero) to 100% (Content at Scale).
entries.source_date: 2023-12-04 (journal publication, International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26); arXiv preprint v2 posted 2023-07-10 (arxiv.org/abs/2306.15666)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; also on arXiv, Weber-Wulff et al., 8 authors including Debora Weber-Wulff, HTW Berlin) -- same underlying paper as EV-detect-01/EV-detect-02, this entry registers the section-5.1.2/5.2.1 cross-tool-disagreement finding on the SAME 14-tool, same-document-set test, which was not previously captured in the registry

entries.claim: A Temple University Student Success Center / Center for the Advancement of Teaching study (dated 2023-08-14) tested Turnitin's AI writing indicator against a disclosed set of 120 texts across four categories (30 each: fully human, fully AI-generated, 'disguised'/paraphrased AI, and hybrid human+AI) and found accuracy fell from 93% on human-written text to 63% on disguised (paraphrased) AI text and 43% on hybrid text, concluding the tool's flagged sections showed 'no relationship at all' to the text's actual AI-written portions. This predates Turnitin's Aug-2025 AI bypasser retrain (EV-turnitin-15) and must be read as describing the earlier classifier, not current behavior.
entries.quote: the summative scores that Turnitin produced for hybrid texts were markedly inaccurate ... there was no relationship at all between sections flagged as AI generated and parts that actually were AI generated
entries.platform: Temple University Student Success Center and Center for the Advancement of Teaching (disclosed-methodology institutional study, PDF report; authors Lori Salem, Stephanie Fiore, Stephen Kelly, Benjamin Brock)

entries.claim: A Feb-2026 peer-reviewed study (Hadra, Cambridge & Mesbah, published in the International Journal for Educational Integrity) tested Turnitin and Originality against a balanced 192-text set (authentic EFL student writing, professional human writing, AI-generated, and hybrid compositions) and found Turnitin's macro-averaged accuracy was 0.61 (versus Originality's 0.69), concluding neither detector 'achieves the level of reliability required for high-stakes decision-making' and that current tools are 'unsuitable as authoritative arbiters of authorship.'
entries.quote: Originality outperformed Turnitin in overall accuracy (0.69 vs. 0.61). ... Current limitations render them unsuitable as authoritative arbiters of authorship.
entries.source_date: 2026 (published online; International Journal for Educational Integrity, DOI 10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1; underlying testing conducted January-May 2025 per the paper's methodology)

Three other detectors tested in the same article (Pangram, QuillBot, ZeroGPT) reportedly identified every sample correctly.
entries.quote: [Undetectable.ai] rated human writing (Test 1) as 60% likely AI, and all three AI writing samples as 75%, 76%, and 77% likely human.

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed academic study tested whether Undetectable.ai could reduce AI-detector scores on GPT-4-generated academic abstracts and found a large, statistically significant drop in AI-detection score after processing (from a roughly 91% baseline to roughly 28% per the study's reported figures).

entries.quote: [search result order for query "zerogpt"]: 1. zerogpt.com  2. gptzero.me  3. zerogpt.net  4. zerogpt.org  5. zerogptai.com  6. zerogpt.tools  7. zerogpt.cc ... zerogpt.plus
